question: What does the German idiom '{{de-DE|Tomaten auf den Augen haben||to-MAH-ten owf dayn OW-gen HA-ben}}' (literally: "to have tomatoes on the eyes") actually mean?
incorrectAnswers: Be too tired to think straight.
explanation: This idiom is used in everyday German for the idea 'Fail to notice something obvious.' Word-to-word: "to have tomatoes on the eyes." Someone with tomatoes on their eyes cannot see what is right in front of them. Example: "Hast du Tomaten auf den Augen? Der Schlüssel liegt doch direkt vor dir." (Are you blind? The key is right in front of you.)

question: What does the German idiom '{{de-DE|Ich glaub, mein Schwein pfeift||ikh GLOWP mine SHVINE PFIFFT}}' (literally: "I think my pig is whistling") actually mean?
explanation: This idiom is used in everyday German for the idea 'Express disbelief or astonishment.' Word-to-word: "I think my pig is whistling." A whistling pig is impossible, so the phrase reacts to news that is hard to believe. Example: "Ich glaub, mein Schwein pfeift! Du hast schon wieder gewonnen?" (I can't believe it! You won again?)
